# 1. PRECEDENTS — twelve buildings, and what each one actually teaches a 20-40 m² kiosk

One correction to the brief before anything else, because an architect on the other side of the table will catch it: **"Ice Watch" was not a Snøhetta project.** It is Olafur Eliasson with the geologist **Minik Rosing** [RECALLED]. Snøhetta's iceberg-adjacent work is the **Oslo Opera House** (2008), whose white Carrara marble roof-plane was designed to read as an ice floe sliding into the fjord. Both are useful; they are different lessons. Getting this right in the deck signals that the architecture section was written by someone who knows the field.

## 1.1 The ephemerality precedents

**Ice Watch — Olafur Eliasson + Minik Rosing (Copenhagen 2014, Paris 2015, London 2018)** [RECALLED]. Twelve blocks of Greenland inland ice, harvested as already-calved free-floating fragments from Nuup Kangerlua fjord, arranged in a clock formation in a public square and simply left to melt. Copenhagen: City Hall Square, ~100 t. Paris: Place du Panthéon, timed to COP21. London: Bankside outside Tate Modern plus a second group at Bloomberg's HQ, ~30 blocks total. The team published a life-cycle assessment for the London edition of roughly 30 t CO₂e to pre-empt the obvious criticism [RECALLED, low confidence on the exact tonnage].

**The lesson is the most important one in this whole report.** Ice Watch works because the ice is *real*, *cold*, *touchable* and *disappearing*. People licked it. The melting was the content. The transferable conclusion for SHABM is the inverse of the founder's instinct: **do not make the building melt. Make the product melt, and make the building permanent.** The cube is the frame; the ice in the customer's hand is the event. Every simulated-melt idea in section 3 is downstream of this.

Second lesson: Ice Watch generated enormous earned media per tonne of ice. A genuine, controlled, public ice-melt event is the cheapest launch marketing SHABM will ever buy. See §3.6.

**ICEHOTEL, Jukkasjärvi, Sweden (1989–)** [RECALLED]. Rebuilt every winter from Torne River ice and "snice" (a snow-ice slurry sprayed over steel formwork), interior held at −5 to −7 °C. **ICEHOTEL 365** (2016) is the permanent year-round wing, refrigerated through the Arctic summer with solar power.

Two lessons. (a) A permanent sub-zero interior in a hot climate is a **refrigeration project wearing an architecture costume** — the sibling's calculation already shows the glass-cube format runs at 0.22 TR/m² against 0.08-0.10 TR/m² for a normal café [source: `Equipment_and_fit-out_CAPEX.json`, in-repo]. (b) The commercially brilliant part of ICEHOTEL is the **annual guest-artist suites**: a new set of designers carve new rooms every season, which renews the press cycle at near-zero marginal design cost. **SHABM should copy this directly — a guest ice-carver residency every summer, one new carved vessel form per season.** It converts a one-time architectural spend into a recurring media asset.

**Icebar by ICEHOTEL London (Heddon Street, 2002–c.2019) and Minus5 Ice Bar (Las Vegas; Orlando)** [RECALLED]. Held at about −5 °C. The business model is a **timed-entry ticketed attraction**: a 40-45 minute slot, a parka issued at the door, cover charge including a drink.

Lesson: the sub-zero room monetises on **admission, not on F&B margin**. Also a caution — Icebar London ran roughly sixteen years and closed. **Novelty-temperature venues have a lifecycle.** SHABM's defensibility must sit in the product and the supply chain (the carved-ice commissary lock already in the model), not in being cold.

Practical translation at SHABM's scale: a full walk-in sub-zero room is out of scope for 20-40 m². But a **3-5 m² "cold cell" photo booth at −10 °C**, entered for 90 seconds, delivers most of the effect. Insulated panel envelope 100 mm PIR + a 1.5-2 kW condensing unit: **$9,000-18,000** [ESTIMATE]. It is also a queue-management device — it gives waiting customers something to do.

## 1.2 The monolith precedents — how to make a small box read as one solid mass

**Kunsthaus Bregenz — Peter Zumthor (1997)** [RECALLED]. This is, in my judgement, **the single best architectural precedent for SHABM and it is not on the founder's list.** A concrete box wrapped in a free-hanging skin of finely etched glass shingles, lapped like scales, with no visible fixings. By day it is a matte block of frozen light; at night it glows from within. Critically, the glass skin is a **separate outer layer**, and daylight is drawn through the cavity into the galleries — the exact double-skin logic SHABM needs for 50 °C (§2.7).

**Lesson: the ice skin must not be the thermal envelope.** Hang it 200-300 mm off a properly insulated inner wall with a ventilated cavity. This one decision decouples the brand look from the cooling bill and is the most important technical recommendation in this report.

**Apple Fifth Avenue "The Cube" — Bohlin Cywinski Jackson (2006; rebuilt 2011; reopened 2019)** [RECALLED]. The 2011 rebuild is the instructive part: the cube was reconstructed from **90 glass panels down to 15**, using ~10 m laminated structural panes. Reported rebuild cost in the region of **$6.7m** [RECALLED, low confidence].

Two lessons. (a) **Joint density destroys the illusion.** At a 3 m viewing distance, a grid of joints reads "cladding"; a small number of very large panels reads "block". Specify the largest panel your fabricator, your crane and your truck can deliver, and detail every joint to disappear (butt-jointed with clear structural silicone, no capping bars, no visible framing). (b) The Cube is a **sign, not a shop** — the actual retail is underground. SHABM's cube can likewise be mostly icon with a modest trading footprint, and the terrace can carry the seats.

**Crystal Houses (Chanel), Amsterdam — MVRDV with Delft University of Technology (2016)** [RECALLED]. A facade of solid cast-glass bricks bonded with a colourless UV-curing adhesive, structurally load-bearing, which **dissolves upward into conventional terracotta brick**.

**Lesson — and this is the single most transferable formal idea in the list: the gradient.** A cube that is dense, solid and opaque at one end and dissolves into void, gap and open frame at the other *reads as melting* far more convincingly than any quantity of running water. Melting is a **loss of definition**, not a wetness. Build the melt into the geometry, not the plumbing. Cost caution: bespoke cast glass is a multiple of conventional facade cost; take the idea, not the specification.

**Prada Aoyama — Herzog & de Meuron (2003)** [RECALLED]. A diamond grid of alternately flat, convex and concave glass panes. The curved panes distort the reflection and the view through.

**Lesson: optical distortion is what separates "crystal" from "window".** A flat sheet of anything reads as a flat sheet. Interspersing a small number of **convex lens panels** (5-10% of the field) into an otherwise flat facade produces the wobble and caustic that real ice has. Cheap to do in thermoformed acrylic: a convex 800 × 800 mm lens in 10 mm PMMA is **$180-450** each [ESTIMATE].

## 1.3 The translucency and light precedents

**Nelson-Atkins Museum "Lenses" (Bloch Building) — Steven Holl (2007)** [RECALLED]. Five translucent volumes of **double-layer channel glass with translucent insulation**, explicitly described as icebergs; by night they glow as luminous blocks of frozen material.

**Lesson: channel glass is the material that most reliably reads as an ice slab at building scale**, because it self-spans vertically with no intermediate framing. No frame = no grid = monolith. This is my headline exterior recommendation for the flagship (§2.6, §7).

**Beijing National Aquatics Centre "Water Cube" — PTW + Arup + CSCEC (2008)** [RECALLED]. A cube of ETFE cushions on a Weaire-Phelan foam geometry, internally lit, glowing blue. Literally a glowing cube of frozen bubbles.

**Lesson:** ETFE gives a luminous cellular cube at a fraction of glass's weight, and it is essentially immune to UV. **But the technology does not scale down.** Each cushion needs edge extrusions and a continuous inflation plant; at 20-40 m² that overhead does not amortise. **Use ETFE for the canopy only, or not at all.**

**Harbin Ice and Snow World (annual, China)** [RECALLED]. Hundreds of thousands of cubic metres of harvested river ice, with **colour-changing LEDs embedded inside the blocks**.

**Lesson:** this is the world's largest controlled experiment in illuminating translucent mass, and its finding is unambiguous — **light injected into the interior of a block beats light thrown at its surface.** Every lighting decision in §4 follows from this.

**Serpentine Pavilions (2000–)** [RECALLED]. 300-600 m² temporary pavilions, built in roughly three months, generating global architectural coverage. **Sou Fujimoto's 2013 pavilion** — a white steel lattice cloud — and **Bjarke Ingels' 2016 "unzipped wall"** of stacked hollow fibreglass frames are the two most relevant.

Lessons: (a) Fujimoto proves **transparency is achieved by layering and lattice, not by clarity.** Three layers of 12 mm acrylic at 60 mm spacing read as a solid block; one 36 mm sheet reads as plastic. **Depth is what reads as ice, and depth is cheap.** (b) BIG's pavilion is a **repeated moulded GRP unit** — the pixelated-ice facade, already solved, and the mould amortises. (c) The pavilion model *is* the SHABM kiosk model: a small, iconic, demountable object that generates media out of all proportion to its footprint.

**Kengo Kuma — Starbucks Dazaifu Tenmangū (2011), Water/Glass (1995)** [RECALLED]. Dazaifu is roughly 210 m² delivered entirely through one material system — around 2,000 interlocked cedar battens — executed with total consistency.

**Lesson: one material, one geometric rule, applied everywhere.** A 20-40 m² box cannot afford variety; variety at that scale reads as indecision. Define a single "ice fracture" surface rule and apply it to the facade, the counter front, the menu board, the tray and the cup. That single rule is the franchise asset (§5.5).

# 2. MATERIALS — what actually survives a Baghdad summer and still reads as ice

## 2.1 The design constraint, stated properly

Baghdad summer conditions used throughout [RECALLED climate norms, corroborated by the sibling's sourced figure of ~134 days/year above 40 °C]: **air temperature 45-50 °C peak, relative humidity 10-18%, direct normal solar irradiance 700 W/m² on a vertical sunlit surface, dark-surface temperatures 70-80 °C, very high UV index, and 20-30+ dust-storm days per year.**

That last one matters more than people expect. **A dusty ice cube is a dead brand.** Dust is the biggest long-term threat to this concept, ahead of heat, and it drives a specific and non-obvious design decision: see §2.8.

## 2.2 Cast acrylic (PMMA)

**Appearance — the best of any polymer.** Light transmission ~92%, higher than float glass. Refractive index 1.49. Castable in genuinely thick blocks and edge-polishable; when edge-lit, thick cast acrylic is the only affordable material that produces a real "light trapped inside a solid" glow.

**UV: excellent — and this is PMMA's decisive advantage.** Cast acrylic is inherently UV-stable without coatings; it is the material used for aircraft canopies and outdoor signage precisely because it does not yellow appreciably over 10+ years [RECALLED]. It will outlast polycarbonate and PETG outdoors by a wide margin.

**Scratch: poor, but uniquely repairable.** Pencil hardness ~2H-3H. It scuffs from a shopping bag. However — unlike hard-coated polycarbonate — **it can be sanded and flame-polished back to clarity in situ.** For a pavement-edge retail object this is a large operational advantage: annual re-polishing of the lower 1.5 m is a maintenance line item, not a replacement event.

**Thermal — the number that catches people out.** Coefficient of linear thermal expansion ≈ **70 × 10⁻⁶ /K**, roughly 7-8× that of glass (~9 × 10⁻⁶ /K) [RECALLED].

> **[CALC] Expansion of a 2,400 mm acrylic panel across a Baghdad annual swing:**
> ΔL = 2,400 mm × 70 × 10⁻⁶ /K × 60 K = **10.1 mm**
> (60 K = a 10 °C winter night to a ~70 °C sunlit surface.)

**Ten millimetres of movement in a 2.4 m panel.** Any detail with a tight through-fixing will craze and then crack, guaranteed, within the first summer. The correct detail is **captive edge glazing in a channel with a minimum 12 mm expansion allowance and no through-fixings at all**; where through-fixings are unavoidable, oversized holes with EPDM bushes. Heat-deflection temperature of cast PMMA is ~95-115 °C [RECALLED], so it is safe against a 70-80 °C surface — but only if you never back it with a dark surface.

**Fire: the weak point.** PMMA is combustible, typically **Euroclass E** (FR grades reach D-s2,d0), ASTM E84 Class CC1/CC2 as a light-transmitting plastic, and it produces burning drips [RECALLED]. **In a UAE or Saudi mall, Civil Defence will not accept standard PMMA on a shopfront.** This is a genuine franchise blocker and is the reason the GCC variant of the design must be glass-dominant from day one (§7.4).

| 20 mm | 23.8 | $95-214/m² | $286-595/m² |

**The 100 mm row is the reason the "solid ice block" facade cannot be built literally.** A 70 m² skin in 100 mm cast acrylic is **$33,000-75,000 in raw material alone**, before CNC, polishing, substructure or installation. The correct move — and this is the core material insight — is **20-30 mm acrylic with deep CNC relief on the inner face and edge-lighting**, which produces the visual depth of a 100 mm block at a quarter of the material cost. [Converges with `Equipment_and_fit-out_CAPEX.json`.]

## 2.3 Polycarbonate multiwall

**Appearance: honest but cheap.** The ribs read as ribs. It only works if you *make* the ribs part of the design — and in fairness, vertical ribs lit from the edge do read convincingly as ice striations. Light transmission 60-80% depending on wall count.

**UV: the problem.** Bare PC yellows badly. With a co-extruded UV layer, manufacturers typically warrant 10 years to a yellowness-index change of ≤6 and transmission loss ≤6% [RECALLED]. **In Baghdad's UV load I would treat a 10-year warranty as an optimistic 6-7 years.** Specify **double-sided UV co-extrusion**, not single.

**Scratch: worse than acrylic, and not repairable.** Hard-coated grades exist (Margard-class) at a premium.

**Thermal: the one genuine performance advantage on this list.** [RECALLED U-values] 16 mm triple-wall ≈ **2.3-2.4 W/m²K**; 25 mm five-wall ≈ **1.5-1.7**; 40 mm ≈ **1.0-1.2**. Nothing else translucent gets near that at this price. CLTE ~65-70 × 10⁻⁶/K (same expansion caution as acrylic). Impact strength is ~200× glass, which effectively eliminates vandalism and hail risk.

**Fire: better than acrylic.** Multiwall PC is commonly **Euroclass B-s1,d0**, self-extinguishing grades widespread [RECALLED]. Malls accept it far more readily.

**Cost** [RECALLED bands]: 16 mm **$18-35/m²**; 25 mm **$30-55/m²**; 40 mm **$55-90/m²**. This is by a wide margin the cheapest translucent square metre available.

**Verdict: the value engineer's friend.** Use it for **the roof/skylight strip and the back-of-house walls** where you need diffuse light without heat, and for the interior of the mall kiosk where fire class matters and reach-height abuse is likely. Do not use it on a hero elevation — it will always look like a greenhouse.

## 2.4 Ice-textured cast resin panels (3form Varia / Koda XT, Lumicor)

**Appearance: purpose-built for this brief.** These ranges include glacier, crackle and ice interlayers with genuinely good depth and diffusion. Koda XT reaches ~25 mm thickness.

**UV: mostly interior-rated.** PETG-based products yellow more than PMMA. Exterior warranties exist on selected products only, and I would not extend a European exterior warranty to Baghdad without written confirmation.

**Fire:** Class A / Euroclass B available on selected products [RECALLED]. **Cost:** **$200-600/m²** at 6-12 mm; Koda XT higher [RECALLED].

**Verdict: specify for the interior only** — counter front, back-bar, menu panel, WC screen. It is the fastest route to a premium interior finish, and interior square metres are few enough that the price is tolerable. Do not put it outdoors.

## 2.5 GRP / GFRP (moulded fibreglass)

**Appearance: opaque or milky-translucent, never clear.** Its value is not transparency — it is **form**. You can mould a 3D melted/faceted/eroded shape at a cost per m² far below carving it from solid acrylic. Every compound curve, every drip, every rounded eroded corner in the SHABM language should be GRP.

**UV:** an ISO/NPG marine-grade gelcoat with UV stabiliser resists chalking; expect a re-gelcoat at **year 7-10** in Baghdad [ESTIMATE]. **Scratch: good hard gelcoat, and — decisively — field-repairable.** A chipped GRP corner is filled, faired and re-sprayed by a boatyard in a day. That is the right property for the base of a pavement object.

**Fire:** standard polyester GRP is Euroclass E. **FR grades (phenolic, or ATH-filled modar) reach Euroclass B-s1,d0** at a **25-40% cost premium** [RECALLED]. Specify FR for anything in a mall.

**Cost:** mould **$3,000-12,000** per repeated panel family; panels thereafter **$120-300/m²** [ESTIMATE].

**Verdict: this is the franchise material.** The mould is a one-time cost that amortises across every store in the network. **Cut the moulds once, in Baghdad or Turkey, and every subsequent store buys castings.** By store 8 the tooling is free and the melt geometry is a brand-controlled component that a franchisee cannot substitute — a soft but real form of supply-chain lock, alongside the carved-ice commissary lock already in the model.

## 2.6 Structural glass, low-iron and channel glass

**Appearance: the real thing, and the only permanent one.** Two non-negotiables:

1. **Low-iron glass (Optiwhite / Starphire / Diamant class).** Standard float glass is green at the edge. In a facade whose entire premise is "this is ice", a green edge is fatal — it reads as a fish tank. Low-iron costs roughly **15-25% more** and is compulsory here [RECALLED].
2. **Texture, not just clarity.** Acid-etched or sandblasted = frost. Kiln-cast / rolled architectural textures (glacier, ice, ripple) = depth.

**Channel glass (Pilkington Profilit / Bendheim Lamberts Linit)** deserves separate billing. U-profile cast glass, installed in facing pairs, **self-spanning up to ~6 m vertically with no intermediate framing** [RECALLED]. Optional aerogel (Nanogel) cavity infill takes the assembly from U ≈ 1.5-1.6 down to roughly **U ≈ 0.5 W/m²K** while staying translucent [RECALLED].

**Because there is no vertical frame, a channel-glass wall reads as one continuous slab of frozen material.** Holl proved it at Nelson-Atkins. This is the highest-confidence "it will actually look like ice" material on the list.

**UV: none. Zero yellowing, forever.** It is the only material here that will look identical in year 15. **Scratch: excellent** (Mohs ~6), and it accepts a sacrificial anti-graffiti film. **Fire: Euroclass A1, non-combustible** — it passes every jurisdiction without argument, which matters enormously for GCC franchising.

**Thermal — and here is the direct conflict the deck must acknowledge.** Baghdad demands a solar-control coating (target **SHGC ≤ 0.27**), but most solar-control coatings are reflective or tinted, which fights the clear-ice look. **Resolution: a neutral triple-silver low-E (SNX-class), VLT ~62-70% with SHGC ~0.27** [RECALLED], plus deep physical shading from a canopy and the ventilated cavity — rather than a heavy body tint. Buy the solar performance with geometry and coating, never with tint.

**Cost** [RECALLED bands]: 12 mm toughened low-iron **$110-190/m²**; 21.5 mm laminated structural low-iron **$300-550/m²**; IGU with neutral triple-silver low-E **$180-320/m²**; kiln-cast textured architectural glass **$400-1,200/m²**; **channel glass, double-glazed, installed $250-500/m²**.

## 2.7 ETFE, translucent concrete, textured PETG, onyx-effect resin, and three materials nobody asked about

**ETFE.** Transmission up to 95%, frittable, essentially inert to UV, self-cleaning (very low surface energy), 25-30 year life, cushions U ≈ 2.0 (2-layer) to 1.2 (3-layer) [RECALLED]. Fire Euroclass B-s1,d0, and it self-vents in a fire. Cost **$180-500/m² installed**, but the inflation plant and edge extrusions are a fixed overhead that a 20-40 m² project cannot amortise; and a 100-250 µm film at reach height on a Baghdad street is a vandalism liability. **Verdict: canopy only, or omit.**

**Translucent concrete (LiTraCon / i.light / LUCEM).** Optical fibres cast into concrete; light points read through a 25-50 mm panel. Durable, beautiful — and **the wrong metaphor.** It reads as *stone that glows*. SHABM needs *water that froze*. Cost **$1,000-3,000/m²** [RECALLED]. **Verdict: reject**, except possibly a single ~2 m² threshold panel carrying the wordmark.

**3D-textured thermoformed sheet — the value play.** A 3 mm sheet vacuum-formed over a CNC-milled "ice crystal" tool gives real 3D relief for **$40-110/m²** after a **$1,500-6,000** tooling charge [ESTIMATE]. Backed by a 10 mm air gap and edge-lit, it throws genuine caustics. **Critical substrate note: use PMMA for this outdoors, not PETG.** PETG yellows within 3-5 years in this UV. PETG is fine indoors, where it also carries a better fire class.

**Backlit onyx/alabaster-effect resin.** Warm, veined, stone-like — the wrong metaphor in summer. But it is exactly right for **winter**: a warm onyx-look panel behind the bar, dark all summer, lit only from November to March, is an elegant physical expression of the seasonal switch. **$150-400/m²** [RECALLED].

Three materials not in the brief that earn their place:

- **Kalwall + Nanogel (aerogel-filled translucent GRP sandwich).** U as low as **0.28-0.85 W/m²K** while transmitting diffuse light, Class A fire [RECALLED]. **$350-700/m² installed** [RECALLED]. It reads as an even glowing plane with no depth — so it is wrong for the hero elevation but **ideal for the north/back wall**, where you want daylight without a single watt of solar gain.
- **Dichroic film (3M Radiant-class).** Shifts from cyan to magenta with viewing angle — precisely the optical behaviour of glacier ice. Applied to glass or acrylic at **$60-160/m²** [RECALLED]. **Highest visual return per dollar of any material on this list.** Use sparingly — 5-8% of the field.
- **Mirror-polished 316 stainless plinth.** Reflects the pavement, so the base of the cube looks like it is standing in meltwater **with no water present.** This single detail does more of the founder's job than the fountain does (§3.5).

## 2.8 The dust decision

Baghdad's 20-30+ dust-storm days per year [RECALLED] interact badly with texture. **A deeply textured outward-facing surface is a dust trap, and within two weeks it is beige.**

**Therefore, a specific and slightly counter-intuitive specification: put ALL deep carving and texture on the INNER face of the outer sheet. Keep every outward-facing surface smooth, and treat it with a hydrophobic/oleophobic easy-clean nano-coating.** You still get the full 3D depth — you are looking *through* smooth glass at a carved surface behind it, which is exactly how real ice presents anyway — but rain and a hose take the dust straight off.

Add to the operating budget: **weekly facade wash, ~2 staff-hours; quarterly professional clean at $60-150/month equivalent** [ESTIMATE].

## 2.10 What I would actually specify — the 60/30/10 rule

**Plinth, 0-450 mm — mirror-polished 316 stainless over honed dark basalt**, sloped. **Roof/canopy — insulated metal deck (U ≤ 0.20 W/m²K) with a 40 mm multiwall polycarbonate or Kalwall strip** washing the interior with diffuse north light.

**And the decision that makes the whole thing viable: the ventilated double skin.**

The ice skin is the OUTER layer. The real thermal envelope is a separate, insulated, sealed inner wall **200-300 mm behind it**, with an open-top, open-bottom ventilated cavity (free area ≥ 10%) so hot air stack-vents out the top.

> **[CALC] What the double skin is worth.** The sibling's cooling model gives solar gain as 20 m² × 700 W/m² × SHGC 0.35 = **4,900 W, 32% of the 15,424 W total load**. Moving to SHGC 0.27 and adding a ventilated cavity that rejects ~50% of absorbed gain before it reaches the envelope:
> 20 × 700 × 0.27 × 0.5 = **1,890 W**. Saving ≈ **3,010 W thermal**.
> At COP 2.8 → **1.07 kW electrical**; over 14 trading hours = **15 kWh/day**; at the sibling's sourced generator cost of $0.15-0.20/kWh = **$2.25-3.00/day = $68-91/month = $820-1,100/year**.
> Capex delta ≈ **$6,000-12,000** [ESTIMATE]. Simple payback on energy alone is 7-13 years — **so do not sell it on payback.** Sell it on the three things that actually matter: (a) it drops installed cooling from ~6 TR to ~5 TR, offsetting **$2,000-4,000** of plant and possibly a genset size; (b) it keeps the ULT freezer inside its 30-32 °C rated ambient, which the sibling flags as *out of spec* in a Baghdad back-of-house; (c) it means the brand can be as transparent as it likes, because **the ice skin is a shading device and a sign, not an envelope.**

# 3. THE MELT DETAIL — the founder's water, honestly assessed

The founder wants water trickling from the base of the cube onto the pavement. I have costed it properly rather than dismissing it, because he deserves the actual numbers.

## 3.1 Water consumption

A convincing continuous *sheet* over a 6 m weir needs roughly **4-8 L/min per linear metre** for an unbroken 2-3 mm film — **24-48 L/min = 1,440-2,880 L/h** [RECALLED rule of thumb]. But melting ice does not sheet; it produces discrete rivulets, which need far less: **0.3-0.8 L/min per metre = 1.8-4.8 L/min = 108-288 L/h.**

Recirculated, so consumption is only what is lost.

## 3.2 Evaporation in 45 °C, 15% RH Baghdad air

Using the standard free-water-surface evaporation relation E [kg/m²·h] = (25 + 19·v) × (x_s − x):

> **[CALC]**
> Ambient 45 °C, 15% RH: P_sat(45 °C) = 9.593 kPa → P_v = 1.439 kPa → **x = 0.622 × 1.439 / (101.325 − 1.439) = 0.0090 kg/kg**
> Recirculated film temperature ≈ 30 °C (a thin film in dry air self-cools toward the wet-bulb, ~24-25 °C here, and settles around 27-32 °C): P_sat(30 °C) = 4.246 kPa → **x_s = 0.622 × 4.246 / (101.325 − 4.246) = 0.0272 kg/kg**
> **Δx = 0.0182 kg/kg**
> At v = 1 m/s (sheltered): E = (25 + 19) × 0.0182 = **0.80 kg/m²·h**
> At v = 3 m/s (open pavement): E = (25 + 57) × 0.0182 = **1.49 kg/m²·h**
> Wetted area: 6 m × 0.5 m apron (3 m²) + 6 m × 0.4 m running face (2.4 m²) = **5.4 m²**
> **Evaporation = 4.3 to 8.1 L/h → 65-121 L/day over a 15-hour day.**
> Add 15% wind drift and splash-out → **75-140 L/day.**
> Blowdown to hold 3 cycles of concentration: E/(CoC−1) = ~50 L/day.
> **TOTAL MAKE-UP ≈ 125-190 L/day = 3.8-5.8 m³/month.**

**So water volume is NOT the reason to say no.** Even at a punitive tankered price of $3/m³ that is **$12-17/month**. The founder is right that it is affordable. He is wrong for four other reasons.

## 3.3 Reason one — Legionella (the serious one)

Key facts [RECALLED — must be verified against the cited documents before this appears in any deck]:

- *Legionella pneumophila* proliferates between roughly **20 °C and 45 °C**, with **optimum growth around 35-46 °C**. Dormant below 20 °C. Progressively killed above 55 °C; at 60 °C, ~90% die-off in about 2 minutes.
- **Transmission is by inhalation of aerosol.** Drinking contaminated water is not the primary route; breathing it is.

**A recirculating water feature in 45 °C ambient sits squarely in the optimum growth band.** Sump water will run 30-40 °C. This is close to a textbook Legionella incubator — and it is a trickling, splashing, aerosol-generating feature at pedestrian level, in wind, directly in front of a queue of customers holding drinks.

Governing guidance to cite [RECALLED, verification targets]: **ASHRAE Standard 188-2018** (*Legionellosis: Risk Management for Building Water Systems*) requires ornamental fountains to be covered by a building water management programme; **ASHRAE Guideline 12-2020** gives specific ornamental-fountain control measures; **UK HSE ACOP L8 and HSG274 Part 3** cover water features as "other risk systems" requiring formal risk assessment; **CDC** explicitly names decorative fountains as a recognised Legionella source and has published outbreak investigations traced to lobby fountains; **WHO, *Legionella and the Prevention of Legionellosis* (2007)** is the base reference. **Decorative fountains are a documented cause of Legionnaires' outbreaks — this is not a theoretical hazard.**

**If you insisted on building it**, the minimum defensible control set is: continuous free chlorine 1-3 mg/L under automated ORP control; 5 µm + carbon prefiltration; UV in the recirculation loop (UV alone is insufficient — it does nothing about downstream biofilm); nightly full drain-down and dry; weekly physical clean of every wetted surface; quarterly *Legionella* culture to a < 100 CFU/L action level; copper-silver ionisation as secondary.

**Cost of doing it properly** [ESTIMATE]: dosing pump + ORP controller + probes **$1,200-3,500**; UV **$400-1,200**; filtration **$500-1,500**; sump, balance tank, pump, drainage, waterproofing **$2,500-6,000** → **CAPEX $5,000-12,200**. **OPEX $150-350/month** in chemicals, testing at $60-150/sample, and staff time.

And after all that you are still dosing chlorine into an aerosol in front of a food queue.

## 3.4 Reasons two, three and four

**Scale and staining — the aesthetic killer, and the argument that will actually persuade the founder.** Baghdad municipal water is hard; TDS is commonly quoted in the 400-900 mg/L range for the Tigris supply [RECALLED — and note the sibling's sourced finding that urban Baghdad households rely on bottled water].

> **[CALC]** Evaporating ~100 L/day at 700 mg/L TDS deposits **70 g/day = ~2.1 kg per month of white calcium crust** — on the exact surface that is supposed to look like pristine ice.

**Within two weeks the ice cube is chalk-white and streaked.** Mitigating it requires RO make-up (the store already has RO for clear ice, but RO rejects 25-50% of feed and costs energy). This alone should end the discussion.

**Slip hazard.** Wet smooth stone at a shop entrance falls below the "low slip potential" threshold easily; the requirement is **PTV ≥ 36 wet, ideally ≥ 45**, i.e. flamed or bush-hammered granite at **R11-R12 (DIN 51130)** [RECALLED]. Iraqi public-liability exposure is thin, but a customer falling in front of a queue with phones out is a brand event, not a legal one.

**Municipal permission.** Discharging water onto a public footway, and occupying it, requires **Amanat Baghdad (أمانة بغداد)** consent on top of the municipal trading licence (إجازة) and the health directorate food licence. Discharge of chlorinated recirculated water to the storm drain is a separate consent. It is probably obtainable — but it lengthens an already 6-10 week licensing path [sibling's sourced figure for LLC registration alone], and **it permanently hands the municipality a lever over the store.**

## 3.5 The safer alternative — four elements that beat the real thing

**(A) "Frozen drip" cast sculpture — the permanent melt. [PRIMARY, always-on]**
Cast the melt itself: icicles, drips arrested mid-fall, and a spreading clear "puddle" set flush into the plinth, all lit from within by embedded LED or fibre so it glistens wet 24 hours a day. **Zero water, zero Legionella, zero slip, zero permit — and, decisively, it photographs exactly like water**, which is what matters when 90% of the audience meets this store through a phone screen.

*Specification:* moulds taken directly from real melting ice. Outdoors, cast in **cast acrylic or kiln-cast glass**, not urethane — **aromatic polyurethanes go amber within 12-24 months in Baghdad UV**, which is a real and common failure. If a urethane is used for cost, it must be an aliphatic system with a UV-stable topcoat. Puddle: 2.5-4 m², 20-40 mm thick, mechanically fixed and grouted flush into a recessed dark basalt apron so nothing is a trip edge.
*Cost* [ESTIMATE]: silicone moulds **$2,500-6,000** (a brand asset, amortised across the network); castings at $350-800/m² × 3.5 m² = **$1,200-2,800**; embedded LED/fibre **$800-2,000**; stone apron and setting **$1,500-3,500**. → **$6,000-14,300 prototype, $3,000-6,500 per rollout store.**

**(B) High-pressure fog — "the cold breath". [PRIMARY, scheduled]**
70-100 bar misting through 0.15-0.20 mm anti-drip nozzles produces 5-10 µm droplets that flash-evaporate in 12-18% RH before they reach the ground. You get **visible vapour rolling off the base of the cube** — which is a *better* metaphor than dripping anyway: it reads as sublimating dry ice and freezer fog, not as a plumbing leak. And it does real work — the sibling's figure is an **8-15 °C drop** on the terrace, which at 45-50 °C is the difference between a usable terrace and an empty one. Since the model puts 44 of the flagship's seats outside, this is a revenue item, not a decoration.

*Legionella note — do not skip this.* Misting systems are themselves aerosol generators. **Single-pass mains-fed only, never recirculated**; 5 µm + carbon prefilter; **automatic purge-on-start** (a pressurised line standing all night at 45 °C is a hazard in its own right); weekly nozzle descale. Softened or RO feed prevents nozzle blockage, which is the number-one failure mode.
*Water use* [CALC]: 25 nozzles × 4-5 L/h = 100-125 L/h when running; on a 3-min-on/12-min-off duty across 13:00-21:00 ≈ 1.6 h of actual run → **160-200 L/day** — comparable to the fountain, but with no sump, no biofilm, no scale on the facade, and an off switch.
*Cost:* sibling's sourced band **$1,300-3,800** for a 60 m² terrace, plus RO/softener feed **$600-1,500** → **$1,900-5,300.**

**(C) Chilled "sweating" panel — real condensation, no plumbing. [GCC-first]**
Run a chilled-glycol coil behind one laminated glass panel so it drops below dew point and genuinely fogs and beads, exactly like a cold glass in a warm room.

> **[CALC]** Baghdad at 45 °C / 15% RH: P_v = 1.439 kPa → **dew point ≈ 12.4 °C.** You would need a surface at ~8-10 °C — achievable but energy-hungry.
> Dubai at 40 °C / 55% RH: P_v = 4.06 kPa → **dew point ≈ 29 °C.** Any surface below 29 °C sweats *spontaneously*.

**So this detail is nearly free in the Gulf and expensive in Iraq** — which makes it precisely the right hero element for the **GCC franchise stores**, and a nice piece of climate-responsive design differentiation between the two markets. Cost [ESTIMATE]: 1.5 kW glycol chiller, pump, coil, insulated panel, condensate tray and drain **$3,500-8,000**.

**(D) Projected meltwater — zero water, night only.**
A concealed IP66 projector at 3 m with a rotating glass gobo throws a slow caustic ripple onto the apron. Combined with the mirror-polished stainless plinth (§2.9), **the pavement looks wet from ten metres away.** Two units at **$600-2,200** each.

**Combined package: $9,000-20,000 prototype / $5,000-11,000 per rollout store** — against $5,000-12,200 capex plus $150-350/month plus permanent legal, hygiene and aesthetic risk for the real fountain. **The alternative is both cheaper and better.**

## 3.6 The answer that actually gives the founder what he wants

Give him a **real melt, on a schedule, under control.**

Every evening at a fixed hour — and at opening, and on launch day — staff place a genuine **25-50 kg hand-carved ice block** on the plinth in a mirrored stainless drip tray **plumbed to the store's own drain, not the pavement**. It melts in public, all night, on brand. It is the store's own product on display. It is Ice Watch at 1/1000 scale.

It is authentic rather than simulated. It creates a **filmable daily ritual** and a reason to come at a particular time. It costs the marginal cost of ice, which this store already makes. It carries no recirculation, no biofilm, no scale, no permit for water on the footway. And when the block is gone in the morning, the absence is itself part of the story.

**This is the single best answer in this report to the founder's request**, and it should be how the melt is presented in the deck: the cube is permanent, the ice is real, and it disappears every night.

## 4.2 SUMMER — "White Ice" (mid-May to end-September)

- **Facade / translucent panels: 6000-6500 K, CRI ≥ 80**, with a deliberate **cyan/blue push** — high CCT alone is not enough; the shift toward 485-495 nm is what makes it read as *ice* rather than as *daylight*.

- **Product and food display — the exception, and it is absolute: 4000 K, CRI ≥ 95, R9 ≥ 90, at 1,000-1,500 lux.** Fruit reds and coffee crema collapse under high-CCT, low-R9 light. The moulded fruit sorbets (strawberry, apricot, blackberry, watermelon) are the most colour-critical objects in the store. **The seasonal scheme must never touch the food light.**
- **Colour accents: cyan ~490 nm and deep blue ~465 nm** at the base and inside the melt puddle. Keep saturated colour to **≤ 15% of the composition** — beyond that it reads as a nightclub, not as ice.
- **Dynamics: a very slow caustic shimmer — 0.05-0.2 Hz, ±10% intensity, randomised per fixture.** Anything faster reads as a fault or a party.

## 4.3 WINTER — "Warm Amber" (November to March)

Same fixtures, different scene file:

- **Facade panels: 2400-2700 K at 60-70% of summer intensity.** The cube stops being an iceberg and becomes a lantern.
- **Interior ambient: 2700 K, CRI ≥ 90, at 250-300 lux** — lower level, warmer, higher contrast, the standard cold-weather hospitality move.
- **Product display: unchanged at 4000 K / CRI 95.**
- Add an **amber 590-600 nm** channel; a candle-flicker emulation at ≤ 5% amplitude on two fixtures only.

**And here is a genuinely valuable brand observation the deck should use.** The financial model already contains a winter hot-drinks line called **كهرمان / Kahraman — "amber."** The winter lighting scheme and the winter menu line are the same word. **The winter lighting scheme *is* the Kahraman brand.** The same physical object reads as a block of ice in July and a block of amber in January, and the menu changes with it. That is a coherent, ownable, seasonal identity that costs nothing extra because it is the same fixtures.

## 4.4 Edge-lit versus backlit — the technical core of the ice effect

This is where most "ice" retail fails, so specify it precisely.

**Backlit (transmissive):** source behind a diffusing panel. Even, flat luminance. Requires cavity depth ≥ 0.5-0.7× the LED pitch to avoid hot-spotting (LEDs at 100 mm pitch need 60-80 mm of cavity). **It looks like a lightbox.** Use it for the logo panel and the menu board — nothing else.

**Edge-lit (total internal reflection / light-guide):** LEDs fire into the **polished edge** of 10-30 mm acrylic.

> **[CALC]** Critical angle for PMMA against air: θ_c = arcsin(1/1.49) = **42.1°**. Light entering the edge within the acceptance cone is trapped and propagates the length of the panel, escaping **only where TIR is broken** — i.e. only where the surface has been CNC-engraved, laser-etched, v-grooved or sandblasted.

**Result: the carved ice-fracture pattern blazes while the rest of the slab stays dark and glassy.** That is exactly the appearance of a beam of light inside a real block of ice — and it is not achievable by backlighting at any budget.

*Practical limits* [RECALLED]: usable throw is ~600-900 mm from one edge in 20 mm acrylic before falloff shows; light **both opposing edges** for panels up to ~1.8 m; beyond that, **gradient the etch density** — denser etching further from the source — to equalise luminance. Expect **30-45%** of injected lumens to emerge from the etched areas.

**The money shot — three offset layers.** A lightly frosted front sheet, a deeply CNC-carved **edge-lit** middle sheet, and a low-level **backlit** rear diffuser, with 40-80 mm air gaps between them. As a pedestrian walks past, the **parallax between the layers** is what makes it read as a solid volume rather than a decorated surface. This costs roughly **2.5× a single sheet**. **Do it on one elevation only** — the one facing the approach — not on all four.

# 5. FORMAT FAMILY — four scales, one geometry

Naming follows the model's existing Arabic convention [MODEL: `المُكَعَّب` al-Muka'ab "the Cube" for the flagship, `الشَّظِيَّة` al-Shazhiyya "the Shard" for the kiosk]. ## 5.1 الشَّظِيَّة al-Shazhiyya — mall kiosk, 12-18 m²

- **Footprint:** 3.5 × 4.0 m island (14 m²) or 3.0 × 5.0 m (15 m²). Height is the fight: malls typically cap kiosks at **2.4-3.0 m**, occasionally 3.6 m for a feature element. **Negotiate height before signing — the cube needs height to read**, and a 2.4 m ceiling turns the concept into a counter.
- **Form:** not a cube. A single leaning faceted **shard** — a fragment broken off the flagship. That is the correct brand grammar for a satellite, and it also dodges the height problem by being diagonal.
- **Seats:** 0 (mall kiosks rarely get seating rights); 2-4 perch stools where the mall permits an adjacent zone.
- **Equipment** [MODEL: kiosk carries no clear-ice plant — carved blocks are delivered from the city Cube commissary, which is the supply-chain lock]: 1× ULT −80 °C **chest** freezer (chest, not upright — better under-counter fit and dramatically better cold retention on door-open), 1× rolled-ice pan, 1× 2-group espresso + grinder, 1× 2-bowl slush, 1× 6-8 pan sorbet display, 1× undercounter blast/holding freezer, 1× insulated bin for delivered carved blocks, 1× undercounter fridge, POS. **Counter run required: 6.5-7.5 linear metres.**

# 6. PACKAGING — ice you can hold

## 6.1 The catch nobody has flagged yet

**Standard clear PET cups become brittle at freezer temperatures and crack.** [RECALLED — PET's glass transition and low-temperature embrittlement are well documented.] The signature **−80 °C "Saqee-80"** drink [MODEL: `saqee80`, $5.23 in Baghdad] **cannot be served in a commodity PET cup.** This is a real product-engineering problem sitting inside the hero SKU, and it is better to have solved it before an investor asks.

Four options:

1. **Heavy faceted glass or double-wall borosilicate, in-house.** Best thermally, best-looking, worst for breakage and takeaway. **$2.50-6.00/unit** [RECALLED]. **This is my recommendation for dine-in** — and it has a strategic benefit beyond aesthetics: it makes the signature drink **a reason to come to the store rather than order delivery**, which is a direct defence against the 15-30% aggregator commission the sibling researched.
2. **Thick-wall injection-moulded PP rated to −40 °C** for takeaway. **$0.35-0.90/unit** [ESTIMATE].
3. **Double-wall clear PP/PET** — insulates (no condensation ring, no wet hands at 50 °C) and looks premium. **$0.18-0.45 FOB China at 100k; $0.24-0.60 landed Baghdad** [ESTIMATE].
4. Reusable/keepsake with a deposit — highest margin, highest operational friction.

## 6.2 Cold-activated thermochromic ink — the best packaging idea available to this brand

**Mechanism:** microencapsulated **leuco dye + colour developer + solvent**, capsules 3-10 µm. Below the activation temperature the dye-developer complex is coloured; above it the solvent melts, separates them, and the print goes clear (or the reverse). Standard activation points available include **−5, 0, +5, +10, +15, +17, +22, +25, +31, +43, +47 °C** [RECALLED].

**For SHABM, specify activation at ~10-15 °C.** The artwork appears when the cup is genuinely cold and **fades as it warms** — the customer literally watches the graphic melt in their hand. That is the brand's entire thesis, printed on the packaging, at a few cents a unit.

**Suppliers** [RECALLED — verification targets]: **Chromatic Technologies Inc. (CTI)**, Colorado Springs — market leader, the technology behind Coors Light's cold-activated mountains and Miller Lite; **LCR Hallcrest** (UK/USA), originators of the modern thermochromic label, "Chromazone" range; **SFXC** (UK); **QCR Solutions** (Florida); **Matsui International** (Japan/USA, textile-grade); and for low-cost volume, **Shenzhen Kingchroma / Hali Industrial / New Color Chemical** (China).

**Cost:** thermochromic ink runs roughly **$60-250/kg** against $8-25/kg for conventional process ink [RECALLED], but coverage per cup is small, so converters quote the uplift: **+$0.02-0.06 per cup at 100k; +$0.04-0.10 at 50k** for one spot thermochromic colour. **It is cheaper and more reliable on a shrink sleeve than direct-printed on a curved cup.**

**The four caveats an investor will ask about, answered before they do:**
1. **UV degradation.** Thermochromic inks fade — expect **6-12 months shelf life** and meaningful degradation after roughly **50-500 colour cycles** depending on grade [RECALLED]. Add a UV varnish. Order in smaller, more frequent batches.
2. **No food contact.** Print outside surface or sleeve only.
3. **Poor batch-to-batch colour matching.** **Never put the brand's core colour in thermochromic ink** — use it for a secondary reveal graphic.
4. Minimum order quantities from CTI/LCR are meaningful; the Chinese suppliers are the route to a 50k pilot.

**Two adjacent technologies worth more than they cost:**

- **Hydrochromic (water-activated)** — the art appears when the cup **sweats**. Poetic, and mechanically perfect for a cold drink.
- **Photochromic (UV-activated)** — the art appears **when the customer walks out into the Baghdad sun.** This works dramatically *better* in Iraq than anywhere in Europe, because the UV load is enormous. **A cup whose Arabic calligraphy is invisible indoors and blazes into view in direct sunlight is a genuinely novel idea for this market**, and it costs about the same as thermochromic.

## 6.3 Faceted and crystal-moulded cups — do not tool yet

A custom injection-moulded faceted cup needs a **4-8 cavity hardened steel mould at $8,000-35,000** from a Chinese toolmaker [ESTIMATE].

> **[CALC] Tooling amortisation:** at **100k units** that is **$0.08-0.35/unit** — more than the cup itself. At **1M units** it falls to **$0.008-0.035/unit** — negligible.
> **Therefore: do not tool a custom cup until network volume exceeds roughly 300k units/year.**

**Two better first moves:**
1. **Buy a stock faceted/"diamond" PET or PP cup** — these exist in the Chinese catalogue at **$0.06-0.14** [RECALLED].
2. **Full-wrap shrink sleeve printed with a facet/refraction graphic** on a stock round cup: **$0.025-0.06 at 100k**, cylinder tooling only **$300-900** [ESTIMATE]. This delivers ~80% of the crystal effect for ~2% of the tooling cost, and it is also the easiest substrate for the thermochromic reveal. **This is the right launch specification.**

**Embossed crystal texture** on a paper sleeve: **+$0.02-0.05 at 100k**, embossing die **$150-500** [ESTIMATE].

## 6.4 Printing Arabic calligraphy on transparent surfaces

**The elegant answer is also the cheap one: matte frost varnish only, no pigment.** A single station of frost varnish on clear PP produces calligraphy that reads as **etched into ice.** It is one "colour", it needs no white underbase, and it is the most on-brand possible treatment. If pigment is used on clear, a **white underbase** is mandatory for opacity — or exploit the transparency deliberately.

**Four Arabic-specific production risks that must be written into the artwork spec** — every one of these is a real, recurring failure in regional print work:

1. **Supply all text converted to outlines.** RTL text reorders, disconnects or reverses when a non-Arabic-aware RIP processes a live font. This is the single most common failure.
2. **Ligatures and kashida (justification elongation) are destroyed if the converter re-flows the text.** Outlines prevent this too.
3. **Verify the plate is not mirrored.** Dry-offset cup decoration sometimes requires mirrored plates. **A mirrored Arabic word is not merely wrong — it is illegible and reads as disrespectful.** Require a wet proof, checked by an Arabic reader, before the run.
4. **Minimum stroke weight.** Arabic scripts have hairline joins between letters. Do not go below **0.25 mm on flexo/dry-offset** or **0.15 mm on UV digital**, or the joins drop out and the letters visually separate into nonsense.

**Process choice:** **digital UV cup decoration** for launch runs under ~20k, where plate charges dominate; **dry-offset** at 100k+.

## 6.5 The frozen-cup sleeve — and a safety item for the risk register

A vessel coming out of a −80 °C freezer will **frost, then sweat, then soak a paper sleeve into pulp** — and at very low temperature it will **bond to bare skin.**

Two requirements:
1. **A corrugated or double-wall sleeve with a moisture barrier** (PE-coated board or moulded pulp), never plain uncoated paper.
2. **A documented service protocol.** The ULT vessel is handled by staff in a **silicone or felt sleeve** and handed over only after equilibrating to roughly **−15 to −25 °C.** The customer never touches a −80 °C surface. **Skin contact with a −80 °C surface causes a cold burn in seconds.**

**Put this in the deck's risk register, and pre-empt the regulatory analogy.** The **US FDA issued a safety alert in August 2018 warning about liquid nitrogen added to food and drink at the point of sale** [RECALLED], and several jurisdictions restricted "dragon's breath" desserts after injuries. **SHABM's −80 °C freezer is materially safer than LN2** — there is no cryogenic liquid, no asphyxiation risk, no product ingested at cryogenic temperature — **but a health inspector in Baghdad, Dubai or Riyadh will reach for exactly that comparison.** Have the differentiation written down before the first inspection, not after.

## 7.3 Performance targets

## 7.4 Maintenance and lifecycle

**Weekly:** facade wash, ~2 staff-hours (dust is the primary aesthetic threat) · **Quarterly:** professional clean, $60-150/month equivalent; nozzle descale on the fog system · **Annually:** re-polish acrylic at plinth height · **Year 5-7:** replace LED drivers · **Year 7-10:** re-gelcoat GRP · **Year 10:** LED L70 reached (50,000 h ÷ 14 h/day = 9.8 yr).

## 7.5 The five decisions that matter most

1. **Ventilated double skin.** The ice skin is a sign and a shading device, not an envelope. Decouples brand from cooling bill; keeps the ULT freezer inside its rated ambient.
2. **Carve the inner face, keep the outer face smooth and coated.** Full 3D depth, but dust washes off. Driven by 20-30 dust days/year.
3. **Edge-light, never backlight.** TIR at 42.1° is what makes a carved panel read as a beam of light inside a block of ice. Backlighting gives you a lightbox.
4. **No recirculating water.** Cast the melt, fog the terrace, mirror the plinth — and set a real 25-50 kg carved ice block on the plinth every evening, draining to the store's own drain. Real melt, controlled, filmable, no Legionella.
5. **One geometry, four scales, one mould family.** The pattern file is the franchise asset — and the reason a franchisee cannot dilute the brand.

open_questions: CRITICAL — nothing in this report was sourced live. Every [RECALLED] price band and every public-health figure needs a real citation before it goes near an investor. The three highest-priority verifications are: (1) the Legionella growth-temperature range and the ASHRAE 188 / HSE L8 / CDC ornamental-fountain guidance, because the deck makes a safety argument on it; (2) channel-glass installed cost at $250-500/m2, because it is the primary exterior material recommendation; (3) cast acrylic $/kg from a Chinese mill, because it sets the ice_skin capex line in the financial model.

Does Baghdad have a fabricator who can CNC-carve and edge-polish 25-30 mm cast acrylic to architectural tolerance? If not, the panels must be cut in Turkey, the UAE or China and shipped as finished components — which changes the landed-cost calculation, the lead time, and the breakage risk. Get three quotes: one Baghdad, one Istanbul/Gaziantep, one Sharjah.

What is the actual maximum panel size that can be trucked from Umm Qasr to Baghdad and craned onto a city-centre site? This governs the Apple Cube lesson (fewest, largest panels). If the practical limit is 1.8 x 3.0 m rather than 2.4 x 4.8 m, the joint pattern must become a deliberate design element rather than something to hide.

Baghdad municipal water TDS — the 400-900 mg/L figure is recalled, not sourced. It drives the scale calculation that is the strongest argument against the water feature, and it also drives RO sizing for the clear-ice plant. Get a lab analysis of the actual supply at the candidate site.

Will Amanat Baghdad permit the mirror-stainless plinth and the cast-resin 'frozen puddle' set flush into the public footway, given they occupy pavement even though they discharge nothing? The melt alternative assumes yes. Confirm before committing to the detail.

Does the flagship site have the structural capacity and the crane access for a channel-glass facade, and is there a regional installer? Channel glass is the highest-confidence 'reads as ice' material but it is an unfamiliar system in Iraq. If no installer exists, the fallback is 30 mm acrylic behind toughened low-iron glass — which is a different, lower-performing and more combustible specification.

Confirm with UAE Civil Defence, through a local consultant, whether ANY exposed PMMA is permitted on a mall shopfront. If it is categorically prohibited, the GCC design variant must be fully glass-and-GRP from the outset, and the franchise pack needs two distinct material specifications rather than one — with a cost delta that has not yet been modelled.

What is the real mall cap on kiosk electrical supply in the target Baghdad and Dubai malls? The Shard needs 12-18 kW connected. If the cap is 10 kW, either the ULT freezer or the rolled-ice pans must be dropped, which changes the kiosk menu and therefore the kiosk P&L.

Get a real quote for the -80 C service vessel. The signature drink cannot use commodity PET, and the choice between borosilicate double-wall (dine-in, $2.50-6.00) and thick-wall PP (takeaway, $0.35-0.90) materially changes both COGS on 30% of flagship revenue and the delivery-channel strategy. The financial model does not currently distinguish them.

Confirm thermochromic ink cycle life and shelf life with CTI or LCR Hallcrest directly. If real-world durability is at the low end (50 cycles, 6 months), the reveal mechanic works for a launch campaign but cannot be the permanent packaging system, and the packaging budget needs a conventional fallback SKU.

The brief asks for a 25-40 m2 flagship, but the format cannot hold a clear-ice plant plus a carving station plus 8-10 m2 of back-of-house below roughly 45 m2 — which is what the financial model already assumes. Decide explicitly: is the 25-40 m2 unit a commissary-supplied format (no ice plant), or is the flagship simply 45 m2? The deck should not show both numbers without resolving this.

Nobody has yet costed the guest-carver residency (the ICEHOTEL lesson) or the nightly ice-block melt ritual as marketing line items. Both are recommended in this report as substitutes for expensive architecture, and both need a budget and an owner before they can be claimed as the media strategy.
